title: Support vector machines as a quadratic program

sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a half-plane</title><line x1="36" y1="168" x2="250" y2="168"/><polygon points="250,168 243.6,170.7 243.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="184" x2="48" y2="22"/><polygon points="48,22 50.7,28.4 45.3,28.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="244" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="18" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><polygon points="70,150 210,40 250,40 250,170 70,170" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.15"/><line x1="60" y1="158" x2="220" y2="30" stroke-width="2.2"/></svg>

sections.body_md:
A linear separator is a hyperplane \(w^T x + b = 0\). The distance from a point to that hyperplane is the absolute value of \(w^T x + b\), divided by the norm of \(w\). For a point with label \(y_i\) equal to \(+1\) or \(-1\), the signed version \(y_i(w^T x_i + b)/\lVert w\rVert\) is positive when the point is on the correct side. The smallest of those signed distances, over the training points, is the geometric margin.

The hyperplane does not change if \(w\) and \(b\) are multiplied by the same positive number. That freedom can be used to scale the pair until the smallest functional margin \(y_i(w^T x_i + b)\) equals \(1\). After the scaling, the geometric margin is exactly \(1/\lVert w\rVert\). Maximizing the margin is therefore the same as minimizing \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\), subject to \(y_i(w^T x_i + b) \ge 1\) for every \(i\).

The objective is a convex quadratic. Each constraint is linear in the unknowns \((w, b)\). The bias does not appear in the objective. It appears in every constraint. The Hessian is the identity on the weight block and zero on the bias, which is positive semidefinite. The program is a convex quadratic program.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The distance and the normalized program are
\[
\frac{\lvert w^T x + b\rvert}{\lVert w\rVert}, \qquad \text{minimize } \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2 \text{ subject to } y_i(w^T x_i + b) \ge 1.
\]
The squared distance from \((x, y)\) to \(p x + q y + r = 0\) is \((p x + q y + r)^2 / (p^2 + q^2)\). Scaling \((w, b)\) does not change a geometric margin.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(w = (3, -4)\) and \(b = 2\), and the point \((4, 1)\). The absolute residual is \(\lvert 12 - 4 + 2\rvert = 10\). The norm of \(w\) is \(5\).

The plaque gap is 2. The distance is \(10/5 = 2\). Multiplying \((w, b)\) by \(2\) would double the residual and double the norm, and the distance would stay \(2\). That is the same cancellation the margin uses. A separator that has already been normalized so the functional margin is \(1\) would report this geometry as a margin of \(1/\lVert w\rVert\), not as the un-normalized residual.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Forgetting to divide by \(\lVert w\rVert\) makes the distance change when the equation of the same hyperplane is scaled. A second slip is to divide \((w, b)\) by the functional margin and then report the new norm as the new geometric margin. The margin is the reciprocal of that norm, and it is unchanged by the scaling. A third is to call the program a linear program. The constraints are linear and the objective is not. A fourth is to put \(b\) into the quadratic objective. The objective is a function of \(w\) only.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The inequalities \(y_i(w^T x_i + b) \ge 1\) are ordinary inequality constraints, so a minimizer carries nonnegative multipliers and complementary slackness. A point strictly beyond the margin gets a zero multiplier. A point on the margin may get a positive one. Those are the KKT conditions of this quadratic program. An equality-constrained stationarity condition is the same balance of gradients in problems whose constraints are equations rather than one-sided margins.
